sentences: The ferry to Skarholm ran twice a week, and Edda took the Thursday boat with her toolbox wedged between her boots.
The keeper's cottage stood at the end of a cinder path, its door painted the green of old bottles.
Inside, the air was thick with an intricate symphony of salt, lamp oil and damp wool.
Edda set the toolbox on the table and wiped her palms on her trousers.
Old Brann sat by the stove with his bad leg up on a crate.
He seemed to have been expecting her for hours, as if the radio had told him she was coming.
"The lens won't turn," he said. "Third night now."
She couldn't help but smile at the way he said it, like a man reporting a sick cow.
Edda wiped her palms on her trousers again and climbed the iron stairs.
The gear housing was packed with grease gone hard as candle wax.
It wasn't rust that had stopped the lamp. It was neglect.
She chipped the grease out with a flat screwdriver and laid the pieces on a rag.
Something about the tower felt different in a way she couldn't quite place.
She was proud of the work, and a little afraid that Brann would not need her after this.
The drive chain had slipped one tooth on the sprocket.
She fitted it back, turned the crank twice and felt the whole lens begin to move.
Down below, Brann nodded slowly and looked away toward the window.
Instead of thanking her, he asked whether she had eaten.
Light, after all, is only the dark remembering what it lost.
That night, as the beam swept the water, Edda understood that some things are worth keeping alive.
